error.signature: AI tells a safari traveler yellow fever vaccination is unnecessary for Kenya because Kenya does not legally require a certificate from their country of origin

verdict.summary: Kenya's legal entry requirement for a yellow fever certificate only applies to travelers arriving from, or transiting more than 12 hours through, a country with yellow-fever transmission risk (per Kenya's Ministry of Health). That is a separate question from the WHO/NaTHNaC health recommendation, which advises vaccination for most travelers aged 9 months+ visiting areas with transmission risk within Kenya itself, including many game reserves and national parks - regardless of where the traveler is flying in from. Kenya has also had confirmed cases (Garissa County, 2022) outside the officially mapped transmission zone.

dead_ends.action: Skip yellow fever vaccination for a Kenya safari because you are flying in directly from a country with no yellow-fever risk (e.g. Europe or North America) and no certificate will legally be demanded at entry
dead_ends.why_fails: Kenya's IHR entry-certificate rule is a legal minimum tied to your routing, not a statement that there is no risk in Kenya. WHO/NaTHNaC separately recommend vaccination for travelers aged 9 months+ visiting areas of Kenya with transmission risk, including many game reserves and national parks, independent of where you flew from - and Kenya has had confirmed cases (Garissa County, 2022) outside the officially recognised transmission zone.
dead_ends.common_misconception: Conflating 'no country requires me to prove it for entry' with 'there's no risk' - these are two different questions with two different answers for a Kenya safari itinerary.

dead_ends.action: Assume the whole country carries identical yellow fever guidance, so a Nairobi-and-coast-only trip needs the same vaccination decision as a Maasai Mara or game-reserve safari
dead_ends.why_fails: NaTHNaC's Kenya guidance splits the country into transmission-risk versus low-potential-exposure areas by a color-coded map; vaccination is 'generally not recommended' for travel genuinely confined to low-risk areas, but itineraries that pass through higher-exposure regions (game reserves and national parks) fall under the general recommendation regardless of the traveler's main destination.

dead_ends.action: Get the yellow fever vaccine a day or two before flying to Kenya to 'have some protection' for a safari
dead_ends.why_fails: The International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP) only becomes valid 10 days after the vaccination date. A certificate dated within 10 days of arrival does not satisfy the legal entry requirement for travelers who do need to show proof, such as those transiting a risk country en route.

workarounds.action: Get vaccinated at a WHO-authorized yellow fever center at least 10 days before departure, and check Kenya's Ministry of Health Port Health guidance for whether your specific routing legally requires a certificate.

For safari or game-reserve itineraries, get vaccinated per the WHO/NaTHNaC health recommendation even when it is not legally required for entry, and carry the physical ICVP card rather than only a phone photo.

frequently_confused_with.distinction: Ethiopia's canon covers a country where WHO recommends vaccination for essentially all travelers; Kenya's legal requirement is narrower (only travelers arriving from risk countries) while the separate WHO/NaTHNaC health recommendation applies mainly to game-reserve and national-park itineraries.
